metadata.title: Is Democracy Overrated? Explaining Support for Dictatorships in Latin America
metadata.venue: IEA Research in Education (Compass Brief No. 7)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This brief uses ICCS 2016 data collected from grade eight students in five Latin American countries (Chile, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Mexico, Peru). The article describes the substantive variables and presents cross-country comparisons (e.g., average civic knowledge by students’ agreement with justifications for dictatorship, and differences by frequency of discussing politics with parents), but it does not report any explicit use of ICCS sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures. Because the manuscript is a policy brief rather than a full technical analysis paper, the weighting and variance-estimation approach is not documented. The results are therefore best interpreted as descriptive/associational comparisons rather than fully specified survey-weighted model estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this brief are students’ agreement with justifications for dictatorship (recoded agree vs disagree) and related indices such as civic knowledge and trust in civic institutions as presented in ICCS reporting. The brief does not describe any plausible-values (PV) generation or PV-combining procedure (e.g., Rubin’s rules) for achievement-like outcomes, nor does it specify whether civic knowledge and trust are PV-based scales or IRT/WLE-based scores. As a result, the PV handling strategy cannot be verified from the provided text, representing a reporting gap for methodological transparency.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used ICCS 2016 grade-eight student questionnaire data from the five participating Latin American countries (Chile, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Mexico, Peru). The brief does not report additional analytic restrictions (e.g., specific subsamples, grade filters beyond ICCS grade eight, or exclusions based on missing questionnaire items). For the dictatorship-justification outcomes, the original four response options were recoded into two categories (agree vs disagree) for clearer interpretation in subsequent analyses.

data.outcome_summary: This IEA Compass Brief analyzes ICCS 2016 grade-eight student data from five Latin American countries (Chile, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Mexico, Peru) to explain support for dictatorships. Across countries, students who justified dictatorship—whether for economic benefits or for order and safety—tended to have lower civic knowledge scores, with Peru showing no statistically significant civic-knowledge difference for the order-and-safety justification. Students who agreed that dictatorships were justified also reported talking less frequently with their parents about social and political issues, with specific non-significant contrasts in Peru and the Dominican Republic. Finally, students who agreed with dictatorship justifications reported higher trust in civic institutions, and the brief argues that the civic-knowledge–trust relationship is complex and varies with perceived corruption/democracy strength. No machine-learning models are trained or evaluated in the provided text; the analysis is based on comparisons and reported statistical significance/correlations.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction targets an official assessment framework, user guide, or technical manual without an empirical ML study. Sample sizes, ML algorithms, and predictive findings are intentionally null or empty per schema rules for non-empirical IEA/OECD documentation.
